Nor would any fair-minded reader accuse Christians throughout history of gnosticism for speaking about the inner work of grace in the heart. Charles’s premise is a classic case of poisoning the well: he asserts what he needs to prove, slapping a derogatory label on Calvin’s position rather than carefully examining what it actually entails. This sloppily asserted premise is the sandy foundation on which his entire critique is built. Indeed, such a method – equating inward conviction with “gnosis” – is so unrestrained that it can be used to falsely argue nearly anything. If one wanted to, one could claim that Catholic mystics, who describe inner experiences of God’s presence, are “gnostics” (they aren’t), or that any person who prays for divine guidance is “gnostically” seeking secret knowledge. The reductio ad absurdum reveals itself: by Charles’s reasoning, Jesus’s promise that the Holy Spirit will “guide you into all truth” (John 16:13) would sound like a gnostic plot. In short, the term “gnostic” in Charles’s article functions as a blunt instrument – a way to prejudge Calvin’s view as heresy without ever engaging its actual content. A sober analysis demands we set the pejorative aside and ask: what did Calvin really teach, and is it as baseless or dangerous as Charles claims? CALVIN’S ACTUAL POSITION: PUBLIC REVELATION & INWARD ASSURANCE Stripped of polemical spin, Calvin’s doctrine of Scripture is both spiritually profound and intellectually nuanced. He maintained that the books of Scripture authenticate themselves by their sublime content and the witness of the Holy Spirit, not by the decree of any human authority. Crucially, this is not a denial of the public, historical nature of the canon – it’s an account of how individuals come to fully trust that canon as God’s Word. Calvin explicitly argued that Scripture’s authority is “derived not from men, but from the Spirit of God,” such that our conviction must ultimately rest on God’s own witness, “namely, the secret testimony of the Spirit.” Only God is a fit witness to Himself. If this sounds radical, Calvin would say it is simply putting God above man: “with great insult to the Holy Spirit, it is asked, who can assure us that the Scriptures proceeded from God… did not the Church regulate all these things with certainty?” he writes, bristling at the idea that “the eternal and inviolable truth of God” should depend on “the will of men.” Calvin’s concern was that if our ultimate confidence in Scripture rests on fallible human institutions, that our faith wobbles on a human foundation. Instead, God must directly certify His Word to our hearts. Far from being an arbitrary assertion, this view arises from a high doctrine of God: only God’s testimony can unshakeably assure us of God’s word. However, and this is where Charles’s caricature misses the mark, Calvin did not throw out evidences, reasons, or the church’s role in pointing to Scripture. In Institutes Book 1, Chapter 8, Calvin painstakingly lists many “secondary helps” that support Scripture’s credibility: the elegant coherence of its message, the antiquity and consistency of its prophetic books, the miracles and prophecies that confirm it, the testimony of the early Church in receiving and preserving it, the unanimity of the godly, and even the heroic martyrdom of those who died for Scripture’s truth. He goes on for pages with historical and literary arguments for the Bible’s divine origin. Does this sound like someone “locked in his own ego” who “disavows the need for reason, argument, and logic,” as Charles portrays Calvin? Not at all. Calvin engages reason and evidence seriously; but he insists these can only go so far. They can render the faith plausible and buttress it, but they cannot generate the full certainty of faith. For that, Calvin says, we need the inward work of God. To see Calvin’s balance, consider his conclusion in that chapter: after cataloguing various proofs, he reminds the reader that such evidences become truly effective only when the Holy Spirit has done His work. Calvin writes, “Proofs of this description [e.g. historical and rational evidences] only [become] of use after the certainty of Scripture has been established in the heart by the Holy Spirit” (Calvin, 1.8). Apart from the Spirit’s assurance, you could pile up arguments endlessly and still not produce saving faith. But once the Spirit “lays that better foundation” of certainty, those arguments and the “consent of the Church” suddenly bolster and enrich our faith with great benefit. In other words, Calvin does not ignore the church’s witness or rational arguments; he simply refuses to let it bear the weight of infallible certainty in the things of God. Charles completely collapses this distinction. He cherry-picks Calvin’s lines about the Spirit’s inward testimony—lines which do sound unapologetically absolute in their insistence on divine assurance—but he omits the context that Calvin elsewhere provides ample “public” arguments. By ignoring Calvin’s own acknowledgment of “evidence of various kinds” that show Scripture to be from God, Charles portrays Calvin as if he offered “zero argument” and expected everyone to take his word blindly. The reality is the opposite: Calvin painstakingly argues on many fronts, but concludes that no argument can substitute for the Spirit’s work in producing conviction. This is a far cry from saying “no arguments matter at all” in a simplistic sense. It is the difference between apologetics and faith; and this is the difference Charles fails to discern. Apologetically, Calvin can and did give reasons for the canon; epistemically, he held that our justification for believing Scripture as God’s Word rests on a source higher than human reason. The distinction between subjective assurance (a person’s confident faith) and objective grounds (evidence and testimony available to all) is critical here. Charles collapses the two, as if claiming an inward source of certainty automatically means there are no objective grounds for the belief. In truth, Calvin would affirm both: objectively, Scripture has manifold marks of divinity and has been recognized by the Church throughout history; subjectively, only the Holy Spirit’s illumination can seal the certainty of those truths in one’s heart. There is no sleight of hand in saying the Church’s judgment is “human” because councils and fathers are humans who can and did err; however, the inward witness is God’s own voice. Calvin’s opponents in the 16th century insisted that the Church’s authority was needed to make Scripture credible; Calvin replied that Scripture is credible in itself and attested by God. One may reject Calvin’s view, but it must be understood on its own terms, not through Charles’s distorted lens. CHERRY-PICKING AND CONTEXT: CHARLES’S ONE-SIDED METHOD A hallmark of rigorous scholarship is contextual fairness; in other words, quoting sources in context and engaging opposing arguments charitably. Charles’s treatment of Calvin fails this test. He lifts quotes from Institutes I.7, such as Calvin’s statement that Scripture “deigns not to submit to proofs and arguments” and owes its full conviction to the Spirit. On the surface, that line could unsettle anyone unfamiliar with Calvin’s broader argument. But a page later, Calvin explicitly clarifies that this refusal to “submit” to proof does not mean Scripture lacks evidence of its divinity. In fact, he says even the learned adversaries will be “compelled to confess that the Scripture exhibits clear evidence of its being spoken by God” when confronted with its majesty and heavenliness. He compares Scripture’s self-evidencing nature to the ability to distinguish light from darkness. Charles mocks this as Calvin merely claiming his view is “obviously right,” but in context, Calvin is describing the way Scripture’s truth becomes clear to a mind illuminated by the Holy Spirit. Charles grabs the metaphor but strips away Calvin’s key point: not everyone has the spiritual “senses” to recognize that light. Calvin, following Augustine, taught that only those to whom God gives understanding can truly comprehend His truth. By cherry-picking, Charles turns Calvin’s nuanced theology into a straw man that sounds like arrogant subjectivism. Consider another example: Charles emphasizes Calvin’s comment that we “ask not for proofs or probabilities” once we rest on Scripture, painting Calvin as anti-intellectual. But in the very next breath, Calvin explains this is not a blind leap but a higher kind of knowledge “which accords with the highest reason.” Here Calvins is arguing that there is a certainty given by revelation that is more secure than any human reasoning, yet not contrary to reason. Calvin even hastens to say he is describing nothing exotic, only what “every believer experiences in himself,” though words fail to do it justice. In short, Calvin’s point is that experiencing the reality of divine truth produces a conviction deeper than intellectual argumentation alone can muster, just as actually seeing the sun gives a more unshakable certainty of its light than any argument about lumens and optics. One may disagree that Scripture offers such an experience to the believer; but Calvin’s integration of experience with reason is hardly the irrational fideism Charles suggests. Omitted as well is Calvin’s acknowledgment that believers still benefit from arguments: once the Spirit has inwardly convinced us, all those external proofs “become most appropriate helps” that “wonderfully confirm” our faith as we reflect on them (Calvin 1.8). This destroys the myth that Calvin tossed aside evidence. He simply refused to let evidence alone be the final basis of faith, since evidence, however strong, still needs the work of God to produce spiritual certainty. Charles’s selective presentation consistently misses these balancing insights. Perhaps most revealing is how Charles handles the Reformed confessions that echoed Calvin. He expresses horror on discovering that Calvin’s view was not a personal oddity but enshrined in multiple Protestant confessions: the 1559 French Confession (which Calvin co-authored), the 1561 Belgic Confession, the 1647 Westminster Confession, and even the 1689 Baptist Confession, all of which teach that our assurance of Scripture’s authority ultimately comes from the Holy Spirit’s work in the heart. Charles calls this a “horrible truth” and implies it’s a gnostic tendency infecting millions of Protestants. But in reporting these confessional statements, he glides over something crucial: each of those documents takes care to affirm the value of the Church’s testimony and many other evidences before stating the need for inward illumination. For instance, the Westminster Confession of Faith, after listing the Scripture’s “heavenliness of matter, efficacy of doctrine, majesty of style, consent of all the parts,” and so on, concludes: “yet, notwithstanding, our full persuasion and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts.” The Belgic Confession likewise says we receive Scripture as holy and canonical “not so much because the church receives and approves them as such but above all because the Holy Spirit testifies in our hearts that they are from God, and also because they prove themselves to be from God.” These balanced statements hardly read as “laughable” or fanatically subjective; they acknowledge human testimony and internal evidence (“prove themselves”) while maintaining that the decisive factor is the Spirit’s witness. By cherry-picking only the “inward testimony” part, Charles presents historic Reformed theology as if it scorned all external evidence; and that is a blatant misrepresentation. In sum, Charles’s method is that of a trial lawyer making a case: quote only the snippets that help your case, ignore context, and press the jury’s emotional buttons. It might win debates in a high school classroom, but it is not how genuine theological inquiry proceeds. A more honest engagement would have to wrestle with why so many serious Protestant scholars over the centuries adopted this doctrine of the Spirit’s testimony. Are they all fools, trapped in “circular” reasoning, as Charles contends? Or did they perhaps find it grounded in the reality of faith and the teaching of Scripture itself? Charles never asks these questions, because he’s too busy scoring rhetorical points by equating Calvin with cultists. NO, CALVIN’S DOCTRINE ISN’T MORMONISM One of Charles’s flashiest comparisons is between Calvin’s view and the Mormon idea of a “burning in the bosom.” As someone who grew up around Latter-Day Saints, Charles recounts how Protestants like himself laughed off Mormon missionaries’ appeals to pray and feel an inner confirmation of the Book of Mormon. He was aghast to realize that, in his interpretation, “Calvin was making the exact same sort of argument” – essentially a Protestant version of “pray and you’ll feel it’s true.” Superficially, the parallel is tempting: both involve inward conviction. But this is a category mistake that conflates two vastly different scenarios. Comparing Calvin’s doctrine to Mormon epistemology is like comparing a surgeon’s lifesaving incision to a random knife wound. It’s true that the superficial form might appear similar (a cut), but the context, method, and outcome are entirely different. First, consider the object of the inward testimony. Mormon missionaries urge people to seek a personal sign confirming a book that holds no prior authority in the Christian tradition. The Book of Mormon, published in 1830, lies outside the historic biblical canon and contains numerous historical and theological novelties. Calvin, by contrast, is discussing the inward confirmation of the established biblical canon: the collection of writings already recognized (with some disputes at the margins) through a long history of use in the Church. The Book of Mormon’s status is the very thing under question when a skeptic is asked to pray about it. But for Calvin, the 66 books of the Bible are not up for renegotiation by each individual’s whim; he assumes the canon that the church at Geneva held (the same 66 that Protestant Bibles contain today) and seeks to explain why believers ultimately receive these books as God’s Word. In short, Mormons seek new revelation; Calvinists rest in historic revelation. The “burning bosom” is supposed to reveal truth that isn’t otherwise evident, whereas the Spirit’s inward witness in Calvin is more about illumining a truth that is publicly evident yet not acknowledged due to human blindness. This distinction is crucial. Calvin never suggests that someone might pray and receive a private revelation to add a lost book to the Bible; rather, the canon is recognized through the historical transmission of prophetic and apostolic writings. The Spirit’s role is to overcome our sinful resistance and dullness so that we recognize those writings for what they objectively are. Secondly, consider the context of community and history. Mormonism’s burning-bosom approach is individualistic in a vacuum: “you can know for yourself,” as LDS President Thomas S. Monson leader put it, by a personal feeling, regardless of evidence or prior community consensus. By Mormon logic, if you pray and feel a warmth about the Book of Mormon, that trumps any archaeological, textual, or historical arguments about its spurious origin. Is this what Calvin teaches about the biblical canon? Absolutely not. Calvin does not ask people to start from zero and invent the canon by subjective feeling. He assumes the providential process by which the canonical books were recognized in the early centuries under the guidance of God’s providence. The fact that Protestants ended up with 66 books was not an arbitrary “burning in Calvin’s bosom,” but largely aligned with the broad Christian consensus on the New Testament and the Hebrew canon of the Old, with the notable exception of the deuterocanonical books that Catholics include. For a fuller historical treatment of the canon question from a Protestant perspective, see my essay: Calvin’s internal witness doctrine operates within the framework of the received canon; it is not a license for each person to privately pick books. Notably, the Protestant Reformers were very conservative about the canon: they did not accept any new books, and their omission of the Apocrypha was grounded in substantial historical reasoning – those books lacked Hebrew originals (for the Old Testament), weren’t accepted as Scripture by Jewish scholars like Philo and Josephus, and had been disputed in the early church. Even Cardinal Cajetan (a Catholic contemporary of Luther) acknowledged the distinction between the Hebrew canon and the Apocrypha. The Reformers, therefore, were not claiming a mystical revelation that, say, 2 Maccabees is not Scripture; they pointed to the public evidence that these books were treated differently in antiquity. What Calvin then adds is that, having weighed the historical and internal evidence, the believer ultimately says “I see and believe these 66 are God’s Word” because the Holy Spirit inwardly convinces him, a conviction which is shared my multitudes of other Christians. It’s not Joe in the pew getting a private list from heaven that contradicts everyone else; it’s the Spirit working in the community of faith so that the church as a whole (in the Protestant view) came to settle on the canonical books. Furthermore, equating Calvin’s doctrine with Mormonism ignores how self-critical and careful the Protestant tradition has been with this principle. Reformed theologians have not used the inward witness as a wildcard to justify wild new doctrines; they have used it to explain the firm trust believers have in Scripture itself. In practice, this doctrine did not lead to Protestants augmenting or subtracting books on a whim beyond the few disputed ones inherited from the medieval period. The same Westminster Confession that speaks of the Spirit’s inward work also lists exactly which books belong in Scripture and even affirms that some books (the Apocrypha) are “not divine Scripture” though they may be useful to read. So, the boundaries of the canon were treated as an objective, historical given. What was up for discussion was the basis on which we are convinced those boundaries are correct. Mormonism’s internal testimonies lead to contradictions with known history (e.g. anachronisms in the Book of Mormon) and with prior revelation. By contrast, the Protestant internal testimony is about confirming a canon that is internally coherent, historically well-attested, and in continuity with the apostolic foundation. The category error Charles makes is treating the means of knowing (inward vs. outward) as the only thing that matters, while ignoring the content and context of that knowledge. It should be obvious that an internal conviction about truth is different from an internal conviction about falsehood. The mere fact that both are “internal convictions” does not make them equivalent or equally valid. As B.B. Warfield succinctly put it, it’s not the psychology of belief that validates it, but the object of belief. Calvin’s inward assurance points to the right object—God’s inspired Word—and thus can be vindicated by its fruits (e.g. leading one to sound doctrine, godliness, and Christ Himself). The Mormon’s inward feeling points to a fraudulent scripture and leads into doctrinal error. Calling them the “exact same sort of argument” is a manifest injustice to the content and outcome involved. In the end, Charles’s Mormon analogy is more revealing of a rhetorical strategy than a theological insight. It’s meant to shock Protestants: “See, your great hero Calvin is no better than those Mormon missionaries you reject!” But this ignores the careful lines the Reformers drew. Even St. Francis de Sales, whom Charles cites as criticizing Calvin on the canon, knew he had to do more than shout “subjective!” to make his case. De Sales engaged in detailed debates about the history of the canon and the status of the Apocryphal books. By contrast, Charles’s drive-by comparison to Mormonism is a cheap shot, lumping together things that share a surface form while differing in substance. It’s the kind of move that may score in a debate club, but it fails as theological analysis. A rigorous refutation of Calvin would need to explain why the Reformed restrained use of the Spirit’s witness is illegitimate, not simply point out that a completely different religion also talks about inner feelings. Ironically, one could turn the comparison around: Latter-Day Saints also believe in a teaching authority (their “General Authorities” and Prophet) who give binding interpretations. Would Charles appreciate Protestants saying the Catholic Magisterium is “the exact same sort of argument” as the LDS hierarchy? Hopefully, we can do better than such shallow parallels. PUBLIC AUTHORITY VS. PERSONAL CONVICTION: WHICH IS REALLY MORE “OBJECTIVE”? Charles frames the issue as private, egoistic faith (Protestant view) versus public, neutral fact (Catholic view). In his narrow view, the Catholic model of canon is clean and historical: an authoritative Church Council decided the list of books, providing a public, external guarantee. Charles argues that Calvin, by rejecting that external guarantee, supposedly “locks the individual inside his own ego… superior to all external witness and authority.” According to Charles, Calvin “sealed off” himself and his followers from “argument, reason, and logic,” making each believer infallible in his private discernment while deeming the entire prior Church mistaken. This is a dramatic story; but does the Catholic alternative truly escape the charge of subjectivity and circularity? And has Charles accurately described the Protestant stance toward history and community? Let’s examine the Catholic model briefly. It’s true that Catholics point to the authority of Church councils such as the Council of Rome in 382, Hippo in 393, Carthage in 397, and finally the Council of Trent in 1546; all of which listed the books of Scripture. Catholics argue that without an infallible Church, we would not know with certainty what writings are truly Scripture. On the surface, this seems appealingly “public”—a council’s decree is open, external, ands fixed in writing. But dig one layer deeper: why should we trust the decree of the Church about the canon (or about anything)? The Catholic answer ultimately invokes faith in the Church’s divine authority. It essentially decrees that one must believe that Christ established the Roman Catholic Church, gave it teaching authority that was protected by the Holy Spirit, and therefore its canon list can be trusted as infallibly correct. But, here’s the catch: accepting that claim is itself an act of faith; one often prompted by an internal conviction or a personal decision that Catholicism is true. The authority of the Church is not a mathematically demonstrable fact; it’s a belief justified by a mix of historical arguments, Scriptural interpretation (“Thou art Peter…” etc.), and an inward sense that this is the true Church. In other words, the individual Catholic ultimately assents to the Church’s authority through a subjective process of conviction—the very thing Charles wants to avoid. A convert like Joshua Charles, for instance, did not attend the Council of Trent in 1546; he read, prayed, and personally concluded that the Catholic Church is right about the canon. His new-found certainty about the canon is, in the final analysis, his certainty; one that resides in his mind and heart, based on his trust in the Catholic Church. That trust isn’t based on neutral logic alone; it’s shaped by faith. He may say the evidence led him to the Church, just as I, a Protestant convert from Catholicism, say that Scripture’s evidence and the Spirit led me to trust the Bible. But evidence alone doesn’t compel belief—many others see the same evidence and draw different conclusions So, ironically, the “public authority” model collapses into an internal conviction as well, except with an extra step: one must first be inwardly convinced of the Church’s authority. The infinite regress is obvious: who assures you that the Church is infallible in defining the canon? If the answer is “Scripture and history assure me,” then one is using evidence and, if one is a believer, likely the Holy Spirit’s guidance to assess that evidence. If the answer is “the Church assures me of its own infallibility,” that’s circular; its essentially saying he Church is trusted because the Church says so—something the Reformers if the 16th century labeled sola ecclesia. In practice, Catholics appeal to a combination of Scriptural and historical motives of credibility and the inner witness of grace to trust the Church. In short, their position is not as purely objective as presented—it involves a large element of faith in an authority, an authority whose credentials one must personally appraise. The Protestant model, by contrast, openly acknowledges that faith is involved in recognizing Scripture. It posits that the Holy Spirit, who inspired the Scriptures, also works in the hearts of His people to recognize His Word. This idea is echoed in Scripture itself. Christ says, “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:27), and the prophet Isaiah writes, “They shall all be taught by God” (Isaiah 54:13)—a passage Calvin also cites. This isn’t a rejection of public authority. Protestants deeply value the public ministry of the Word, the historic traditions of the Church, and the Church’s ministerial authority as the context in which individuals are brought to recognize and receive Scripture. Reformed theologian Francis Turretin in the 17th century spoke of the Church as the organ by which God hands down Scripture, though not the source of Scripture’s authority. In fact, Calvin himself credited the early Church councils and fathers with faithfully (if not infallibly) passing down the true canon. He praised, for example, Augustine’s agreement on the core New Testament writings, even if Augustine included the apocryphal books in his list. The difference is that Protestants ultimately give thanks to the Church and obedience to the Word. The Church’s role is ministerial, not magisterial, in the recognition of Scripture. And crucially, Protestants believe that the same Spirit who guided the process of canonization externally must guide acceptance of the canon internally. Charles’s portrayal of “1,500 years of Christians” versus “Calvin’s small sect” can only be described as melodramatic. He implies that Calvin set himself against the entire prior tradition of the church, arbitrarily excluding books that all earlier saints accepted. But history is more complicated than he suggests. Yes, from the late 4th century on, the Western Church mostly used the larger canon including the deuterocanonical books; although with some continued caveats by scholars like Jerome. However, the Eastern Church to this day has a slightly different Old Testament canon (e.g. the Ethiopic Church includes books like Enoch; the Greek Church did not firmly dogmatize the exact list). It’s important to note that during the first 500 years of Christianity, various Church Fathers expressed doubts about books like Esther, Revelation, 2 Peter and the deuterocanonical books. So, the “public witness” was not as monolithic as Charles suggests. The Council of Trent’s 1546 decision to affirm the canonicity of the Apocrypha—in response to Protestant objections—was not without significant internal debate. A large number of bishops favored excluding some of the deuterocanonical books, though the majority ultimately voted to include all seven. My point is not to adjudicate that debate here, but to show that Calvin wasn’t simply thumbing his nose at an uncontested fact. He was aligning with the Hebrew Bible canon and the view of many early Jews and Christians that the Apocrypha were beneficial but not equal to inspired Scripture. We see Calvin’s historical awareness when he notes that even the ancient Church made distinctions; he was not, contrary to Charles’s assertion, saying that all Christians before him were blind and only he and his friends had their “senses working properly.” Rather, Calvin would argue that whenever those earlier Christians truly heard God’s voice in Scripture, it was by the same Spirit’s illumination he now extols, even if they did not articulate the doctrine formally. Finally, Charles’s insistence that Calvin’s view makes the individual “infallible” and the Church “not” is a gross distortion. Calvin never says individuals become infallible. Individuals can err; they can even mistakenly think they have the Spirit’s witness when they do not; which ironically is why Protestants emphasize testing alleged revelations against Scripture itself. The inward testimony of the Spirit is not a new proposition or separate revelation; it doesn’t tell you “Book X is canonical” in a vacuum. Rather, as the Westminster Confession says, the Spirit “bears witness by and with the Word in our hearts.” That is, as one reads or hears the Word, the Spirit works to elicit faith in it. It’s a concurrent action, not a secret voice dictating a list of books on a desert island. Here Calvin stands in continuity with Augustine, who taught that divine grace is necessary not only to will the good but to perceive and embrace the truth. In Grace and Free Will (ch. 33), Augustine writes: “It is God who works in us not only the bringing to pass what we know we ought to do, but also the very knowing itself.” Augustine does not pit divine illumination against public revelation, but shows that even the capacity to assent to revealed truth is a gift of grace. Calvin, following this Augustinian line, insists that the certainty with which believers receive Scripture is not self-generated; it is the work of God, the same God who cannot lie. Augustine of Hippo, Image by Wikipedia So when the Spirit bears witness, the assurance that follows is well-grounded — not because the individual becomes infallible, but because God assures the heart, and God does not lie. The believer’s certainty rests not on internal psychology but on divine grace operating through the Word. This “inward testimony” is not a shortcut around the Church, tradition, or Scripture, but the means by which the soul is enabled to truly receive what God has publicly revealed. Charles’s portrayal of it as a self-authenticating ego-trip ignores both Calvin’s careful theology and Augustine’s profound insight: faith itself is God’s work in us; and even our seeing is by grace. But any given person might be self-deceived, which is why the Reformers did not urge believers to ignore the broader Church. On the contrary, they expected true believers to substantially agree on the canon because the same Spirit was at work in all. This is largely what happened; Protestants across Europe coalesced on the same canon, independently of any centralized authority, which from their view vindicated the work of the Spirit. If one Protestant had started advocating for Shepherd of Hermas or 3 Corinthians as Scripture, the others would have rejected that as an aberration, because it lacked the shared witness of the Spirit and the historical pedigree. In practice, the internal witness doctrine produced unity around the core canon, not fragmentation. Charles’s nightmare of every individual sealed in a solipsistic bubble just isn’t the reality of how Protestant churches functioned. They had a high view of the collective “sense of the faithful” (sometimes called the testimonium commune of the Spirit), not just individual intuition. In reality, both Catholic and Protestant models involve elements of the public and the private, the external and the internal. The Catholic affirms the visible Church’s testimony and assents to it through an inner act of faith that the Church is trustworthy. The Protestant trusts the Scripture’s testimony, moved by an inner faith given by the Spirit that these Scriptures are God’s own. Both recognize that if God doesn’t enlighten, the human mind remains unconvinced (Catholic theology too says faith is a gift of the Holy Spirit). The difference lies in what is considered the ultimate channel of God’s assurance; the Church or the Scripture itself. Charles portrays the Catholic channel as if it required no faith (just history) and the Protestant channel as if it admitted no evidence (just feeling). Both portrayals are false dichotomies. A fairer comparison would admit that historical evidence and spiritual illumination play roles in both systems but are weighted differently. Charles’s black-and-white narrative obscures this reality. POLEMICS VS. SCHOLARSHIP: A CASE STUDY IN CONTRAST Perhaps the most striking aspect of Charles’s article is the tone and method: it is a textbook example of apologetic polemic masquerading as analysis. This merits attention not to make an ad hominem attack on Charles, but to caution readers on the difference between rhetorical persuasion and scholarly argumentation. Charles writes as a lawyer might prosecute a case. He heaps strong words on Calvin’s position – “laughable,” “absurd,” “gnostic,” “horrible truth,” “novel form of Gnosticism under a veneer of Christianity”—and uses vivid imagery (Calvin locking himself in an ego vault, etc.) to sway the reader emotionally. He sets up dire-sounding questions: “What could be more absurd than this? Is anything like this found in Christian history? … The answer… is ‘nothing.’” These are bold claims indeed. But step back: this is not the language of careful historical or theological scholarship. It’s the language of a debater or a pamphleteer. A scholar examining Calvin’s view of the canon would ask nuanced questions: How did Calvin build on earlier theologians like Augustine; who also emphasized the role of the Spirit and the intrinsic power of Scripture? In what context did Calvin feel the need to stress the Spirit’s testimony? Recall that it was in public debate with Roman Catholic apologists of his day who argued Scripture’s authority derives from the Church? How did Calvin’s contemporaries and successors interpret and perhaps refine this doctrine? What are the potential weaknesses or strengths of the position? None of these avenues are explored in Charles’s piece. Instead, he employs a kind of shock-and-awe tactic: find a startling angle (Calvin = gnostic = like Mormonism), repeat it often, and conclude that the opponent’s view is beyond the pale. This approach may fire up partisans, but it fails as serious analysis. For one, it assumes what needs to be proven. Calling Calvin’s argument “entirely private (i.e. gnostic) and completely circular” is not an argument, it’s a conclusion stated in emphatic terms. A fair analysis would define gnosticism and circular reasoning carefully and then see if Calvin truly fits those definitions. Charles does not bother. He uses “gnostic” as an epithet, not a defined term. On circularity: any fundamental authority claim (whether “Scripture is God’s Word” or “the Church is infallible”) can be accused of circularity because ultimately one appeals to that authority to authenticate itself in some way. A more thoughtful discussion would recognize this philosophical challenge and see how each side addresses it. But Charles simply slaps the label “circular” on Calvin and presumes the case closed. Ironically, by refusing to engage the self-authenticating concept of Scripture on its own terms, Charles traps himself in a circular method of his own: he presupposes that an internal witness must be invalid, because if it weren’t, his Catholic position would falter. So, without proving it invalid, he just declares it so. Charles’s academic credibility also suffers from his cavalier handling of sources. We have already seen how he quotes Calvin without context. This is not the practice of a scholar seeking truth; it’s what one does when building a polemical brief. He also seems unaware (or uninterested) in how Protestant theologians themselves have addressed the very objections he raises. For example, the analogy to Mormonism or subjective delusion is hardly new—Protestants have long explained why “the inward testimony of the Spirit” is not equivalent to fanaticism or new private revelation. The Westminster divines in the 1640s took care to say the Spirit’s witness is by and with Scripture – anchoring it objectively in God’s inspired Word. Reformed apologist William Whitaker in the 16th century distinguished between the authority of Scripture in itself (which is absolute) and the means by which we come to know that authority; emphasizing the internal work of the Spirit in the latter. If Charles were engaging in genuine scholarship, he would at least acknowledge these clarifications and perhaps try to rebut them. Instead, he writes as if he’s the first to discover this “horrible truth” and as if Protestants themselves have been too blind to notice the alleged gnostic implications. This lack of engagement with the broader academic discussion indicates a confirmation bias at work: Charles has a narrative (Protestantism leads to subjectivism), and he selects and interprets data only to fit that narrative. It’s notable that he leans heavily on St. Francis de Sales, a famous Catholic polemicist, as if an opponent’s polemic is the last word on the matter. A more balanced review would incorporate Protestant voices or at least neutral scholarly voices on Calvin. By ignoring them, Charles shows his proclivity to produce advocacy journalism with a foregone conclusion and then call it analysis. It’s not theology; it’s courtroom theatrics dressed up as scholarship—complete with selective citations, loaded labels, and a verdict rendered before the evidence is fairly heard. None of this is to say that sharp polemic has no place. The history of theology indeed has its polemical side. In fact, Calvin can be scathing in tone about the Pope or the “fanatics” (the radical Spiritualists of his day), yet he also reasoned through scriptural and historical evidence at length. In Charles’s article, the ratio of heat to light leans heavily toward heat. The few substantive points he raises—such as the Mormon analogy or the quip about Protestant disunity—are underdeveloped and easily addressed. As we’ve seen, the Mormon comparison is a category error, and doctrinal variation among Protestants does not undermine their shared conviction about the canon; unity in one area does not require uniformity in all. Instead of strengthening these arguments, Charles resorts to piling on adjectives like “absurd,” “incoherent,” and “impossible to imagine anything more gnostic,” as if rhetoric could do the work of reasoning. This is the telltale sign of persuasion by volume rather than persuasion by evidence. For Protestant and open-minded Catholics readers, the takeaway should be a caution: don’t mistake bombast for truth. A calm, careful reading of Calvin—and of the Reformed confessions—shows a view that is honestly trying to uphold both the role of the Church and the primacy of God’s action in giving us confidence in His Word. You may disagree with that view, but it’s hardly an outrageous, anti-rational, or cultic position. It actually resonates with deep Augustinian theology and his statement: “I believe in order to understand”—indicating that faith illumines reason. A serious critic would grapple with those nuances. Charles chose the easier path of caricature. In doing so, he provided a case study in the difference between rigorous theological scholarship and one-sided apologetic polemic. The former illuminates, the latter obfuscates. Unfortunately for Charles’s readers, he delivered the latter. CONCLUSION: PUBLIC TRUTH, INWARDLY CONFIRMED At its heart, the question of how we know the canon of Scripture comes down to the interplay of the external and the internal, the objective and the subjective; or, one could say, the divine and the human. John Calvin and the Protestant tradition maintain that Scripture is objectively God’s Word, given through the public, apostolic channels of history, and that God the Holy Spirit works subjectively in human hearts to fully persuade us of that fact. These two truths are not at odds: the Holy Spirit is the author of the public revelation and the illuminator of our minds to receive it. This “internal witness” doctrine does not make Scripture any less publicly revealed; it simply acknowledges that recognizing divine authority is ultimately a spiritual act. As the Belgic Confession beautifully states, the Church may present and honor the Scriptures, but “above all because the Holy Spirit testifies in our hearts that they are from God, and also because they prove themselves to be from God” we receive them as canonical. Notice the balance: the books prove themselves (objectively) and the Spirit testifies in our hearts (subjectively). There is nothing gnostic in this balance; it has been the experience of mainstream Christianity that faith involves both evidence and the work of God within. Joshua Charles’s attempt to refute Calvin by dubbing the his canon theory “gnostic” fails to land a serious blow. It fires the imagination with provocative comparisons and strong words, but ultimately it does little more than knock down a straw man of Charles’s own making. The core premise of his article—that an inward witness of the Spirit is a gnostic, wildly subjective free-for-all—is factually and theologically unsupported and false. Calvin’s appeal to the Spirit was in fact an appeal to God’s own active fidelity: the belief that the God who inspired the Scriptures has not left His people dependent on uncertain human opinion, but actively “seals” the truth of Scripture on the hearts of believer. This doctrine was not Calvin’s eccentricity; it became the common confession of Reformed churches because it rings true to both Scripture and experience. Yes, it is offensive to purely natural reason that we should depend on the invisible Spirit to certify God’s Word. but it is equally offensive to Protestant ears that one should depend on an ostensibly infallible human institution. At the end of the day, both Protestants and Catholics trust God to guide His Church into recognizing His Word; they just differ on the mechanism (directly by the Spirit through Scripture, or mediately by the Spirit through a magisterium). Simply calling one “gnostic” is an insult, not an argument. The difference between apologetic rhetoric and genuine scholarship becomes evident in controversies like this. Charles’s rhetoric might score a momentary win among partisans or the less informed, but it does not hold up under careful analysis. A rigorous approach would have acknowledged the legitimate concerns Calvin raised: the need for an unshakeable foundation for faith, the insufficiency of human authority, and the biblical precedent for God’s direct illumination. It also would have examined Catholic claims with equal scrutiny, recognizing that appealing to Church authority raises its own epistemic questions. Instead, Charles gave us a cautionary tale in confirmation bias and polemical excess. Protestants can take some solace in the fact that if our opponents must resort to such tactics, perhaps our position is more resilient than they care to admit. In the final analysis, John Calvin’s doctrine of the inward witness of the Holy Spirit stands not as a kooky outlier to be mocked, but as a thoughtful attempt to articulate how objective divine truth becomes subjectively certain in the hearts of God’s people. It does not undermine the public, historical nature of the Christian faith; rather, it assures that the public truth is truly received as truth and not merely as one opinion among others. There is nothing either absurd or novel in this. Rather, it reflects the consistent witness of historic Christianity: that faith itself is not self-generated, but a gift of God—graciously given, spiritually illumined, and anchored in truth. As readers and believers, we should examine the rational grounds for our trust in Scripture, but we should also humbly acknowledge that if we truly believe the Bible is God’s Word, it is because God Himself has impressed that truth upon us. hat is not gnostic escapism; it is, in fact, a point on which Catholic and Protestant piety quietly agree: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6:44). The recognition of divine truth—whether in Scripture or in Christ Himself—is ultimately a gift of grace, not a product of unaided human judgment. It is fitting, then, to close by emphasizing that the Protestant view of the canon, properly understood, upholds both the external witness and the internal Witness; the venerable testimony of the Church and the sovereign testimony of the Spirit. Joshua Charles’s critique might make for a fiery Substack read, but when it comes to substance, it is wood, hay, and stubble. The Protestant doctrine of Scripture’s self-authentication by the Holy Spirit’s inward work, by contrast, rests on the solid rock of God’s promised faithfulness – a foundation no amount of polemical tempest can erode. passage: Venetian painting Venetian painting was a major force in Italian Renaissance painting and beyond. Beginning with the work of Giovanni Bellini (c. 1430–1516) and his brother Gentile Bellini (c. 1429–1507) and their workshops, the major artists of the Venetian school included Giorgione (c. 1477–1510), Titian (c. 1489–1576), Tintoretto (1518–1594), Paolo Veronese (1528–1588) and Jacopo Bassano (1510–1592) and his sons. Considered to give primacy to colour over line,[1] the tradition of the Venetian school contrasted with the Mannerism prevalent in the rest of Italy. The Venetian style exerted great influence upon the subsequent development of Western painting.[2] By chance, the main phases of Venetian painting fit rather neatly into the centuries. The glories of the 16th century were followed by a great fall-off in the 17th, but an unexpected revival in the 18th,[3] when Venetian painters enjoyed great success around Europe, as Baroque painting turned to Rococo. This had ended completely by the extinction of the Republic of Venice in 1797 and since then, though much painted by others, Venice has not had a continuing style or tradition of its own.[4] Though a long decline in the political and economic power of the Republic began before 1500, Venice at that date remained "the richest, most powerful, and most populous Italian city"[5] and controlled significant territories on the mainland, known as the terraferma, which included several small cities who contributed artists to the Venetian school, in particular Padua, Bergamo, Brescia and Verona. The Republic's territories also included Istria, Dalmatia and the islands now off the Croatian coast, who also contributed. Indeed, "the major Venetian painters of the sixteenth century were rarely natives of the city" itself,[6] and some mostly worked in the Republic's other territories, or further afield.[7] The rest of Italy tended to ignore or underestimate Venetian painting; Giorgio Vasari's neglect of the school in the first edition of his Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects in 1550 was so conspicuous that he realized he needed to visit Venice for extra material in his second edition of 1568.[8] In contrast, foreigners, for whom Venice was often the first major Italian city visited, always had a great appreciation for it and, after Venice itself, the best collections are now in the large European museums rather than other Italian cities. At the top, princely, level, Venetian artists tended to be the most sought after for commissions abroad, from Titian onwards, and in the 18th century most of the best painters spent significant periods abroad, generally with great success.[9] Media and techniques [edit]Venetian painters were among the first Italians to use oil painting,[10] and also to paint on canvas rather than wooden panels. As a maritime power good quality canvas was always available in Venice, which was also beginning to run rather short of timber. The large size of many Venetian altarpieces (for example Bellini's San Zaccaria Altarpiece of 1505, originally on panel) and other paintings encouraged this, as large panel surfaces were expensive and difficult to construct. The Venetians did not develop a "native school" of fresco painting, often relying on Padua and Verona, Venetian from 1405, to supply painters (notably Paolo Veronese). They continued to add gold ground mosaics to San Marco long after the rest of Europe had abandoned the medium. Somewhat perversely, they were happy to add frescos to the outside of palazzi, where they deteriorated even faster than elsewhere in Italy, and have only left a few shadowy traces, but apart from the Doge's Palace, used them little in other interior settings. The rapid deterioration of external frescos is often attributed to the seaside Venetian climate, perhaps wrongly.[11] Probably partly for this reason, until the 18th century (with rare exceptions) Venetian churches were never given a coherent scheme of decoration, but feature a "rich profusion of different objects in a picturesque confusion", often with much wall space taken up by grandiose wall-tombs.[12] Compared with Florentine painting, Venetian painters mostly used and have left fewer drawings.[13] Perhaps for this reason, and despite Venice being Italy's largest centre of printing and publishing throughout the Italian Renaissance and for a considerable time afterwards, the Venetian contribution to printmaking is less than might be expected. Like Raphael, Titian experimented with prints, using specialist collaborators, but to a lesser extent. The engraver Agostino Veneziano moved to Rome in his twenties, and Giulio Campagnola and his adoptive son Domenico Campagnola are the main 16th-century artists who concentrated on printmaking and remained in the Republic of Venice, apparently mostly in Padua.[14] The situation was different in the 18th century, when both Canaletto and the two Tiepolos were significant etchers, and Giovanni Battista Piranesi, though famous for his views of Rome, continued to describe himself as a Venetian for decades after moving to Rome.[15] Early development, to 1500 [edit]14th century [edit]Paolo Veneziano, probably active between about 1320 and 1360, is the first major figure we can name, and "the founder of the Venetian school". He seems to have introduced the "composite altarpiece" of many small scenes within an elaborate gilded wooden frame, which remained dominant in churches for two centuries. These transferred to painting the form of the huge, jewel-encrusted and very famous Pala d'Oro behind the main altar in San Marco, the enamel panels for which had been made in, and later looted from, Constantinople for successive doges.[16] In fact, one of Veneziano's commissions was to paint "weekday" panels to fit over the Pala, which was only revealed for feast-days. His style shows no influence from Giotto, active a generation earlier.[17] The earliest form of Italian Renaissance painting was first seen in Venice when Guariento di Arpo from Padua was commissioned to paint frescos in the Doge's Palace in 1365. 15th century [edit]The traditional Italo-Byzantine style persisted until around 1400 when the dominant style began to shift towards International Gothic, with Jacobello del Fiore a transitional figure and the trend, which continued in the rather charming work of Michele Giambono (c. 1400 – c. 1462), who also designed mosaics for San Marco. Gentile da Fabriano and Pisanello were both in Venice during much of the years 1405–1409, painting frescos (now lost) in the Doge's Palace and elsewhere.[18] By the mid-century, when the Florentine quattrocento was fully mature, Venice still lagged well behind. Perhaps the most visible work in Venice in the Tuscan style was a mosaic Death of the Virgin, in the Capella Mascoli in San Marco, next to a design by Gambono, though other works in the city included frescos by Andrea Castagno.[19] The Vivarini and Bellini families were the two major dynasties of 15th-century painters in the city, and the Vivarini, though in the end more conservative, were initially the first to embrace styles from the south.[20] Carlo Crivelli (c. 1430–1495) was born in the city, but spent his mature career outside the Republic's territories. His style – highly individual, rather linear, and somewhat neurotic – had no influence on later Venetian painting.[21] From the late-15th century, Venetian painting developed through links with Andrea Mantegna (1431–1506) (from nearby Padua) and of a visit by Antonello da Messina (c. 1430–1479), who introduced the oil painting technique of Early Netherlandish painting, probably acquired through his training in Naples.[22] Another external factor was the visit by Leonardo da Vinci, who was particularly influential on Giorgione.[23] During his long career, Giovanni Bellini has been credited with creating the Venetian style.[2] After earlier works, such as his Madonna of the Small Trees (c. 1487), which largely reflect the linear approach of Mantegna, he later developed a softer style, where glowing colours are used to represent form and suggest an atmospheric haze. Applying this approach in his San Zaccaria Altarpiece (1505), the high viewpoint, the uncluttered and interconnected figures arranged in space, and the subtle gestures all combine to form a tranquil yet majestic image.[24] With such works he has been described as reaching the High Renaissance[24] ideals, and certainly expresses the key distinctive factors of the Venetian school. Vittore Carpaccio (c. 1465–1525/1526) was a pupil of Bellini, with a distinct style. He was rather conservative, and ignored the High Renaissance style developing in the later part of his career, indeed retaining a Late Gothic poetry in many works. With Gentile Bellini, many of Carpaccio's large works give us famous scenes of contemporary life in the city; at this period such views were unusual. He was one of the first painters to mostly use canvas rather than panels. There were a number of other painters who continued essentially quattrocento styles in the two decades after 1500; Cima da Conegliano (c. 1459–c. 1517) is the most significant.[25] 16th century [edit]Giorgione and Titian [edit]Giorgione and Titian were both apprentices at Bellini's workshop. A speciality of Giorgione's were idyllic Arcadian scenes, with an example being his Three Philosophers, and this element was adopted by his master Bellini, who increased the landscape in his many Madonnas,[26] and by Titian in work like Pastoral Concert (1508) and Sacred and Profane Love (1515). This emphasis on nature as a setting was a major contribution of the Venetian School. Titian, through his long and productive life, with a wide variety of themes and subjects was the most influential and greatest of all the Venetian painters.[27][28] His early Pesaro Madonna (1519–1528) shows a bold new composition for such a traditional religious subject,[29] putting the focal point of the Madonna off from the centre and on a steep diagonal. Colours are used to enliven the painting, but also to unify the composition, such as by the large red flag on the left counterbalancing the red in the Madonna[30] and such skilful and sumptuous use of colour became a hallmark of the Venetian style. Although pre-figured by the Sleeping Venus (completed by Titian after Giorgione's death in 1510) Titian is credited with establishing the reclining female nude as an important subgenre in art. Using mythological subjects, works such as the Venus of Urbino (1538) richly depict the fabrics and other textures, and use a composition that is carefully controlled by organising colours. As an example, in this painting the diagonal of the nude is matched by the opposite diagonal between the red of the cushions in the front with the red skirts of the woman in the background.[31] With other Venetian painters such as Palma Vecchio, Titian established the genre of half-length portraits of imaginary beautiful women, often given rather vague mythological or allegorical titles, with attributes to match. The artists apparently did nothing to discourage the belief that these were modelled for by the most celebrated of Venice's famous courtesans, and sometimes this may have been the case. Titian continued to paint religious subjects with growing intensity, and mythological subjects, which produced many of his most famous later works, above all the poesie series for Philip II of Spain. With such paintings, readily transported by virtue of being oils on canvas, Titian became famous, and helped establish a reputation for Venetian art. Possession of such paintings symbolised luxurious wealth,[32] and for his skills in portraiture he was sought by powerful, rich individuals, such as in his long relationship working for Emperor Charles V and Philip II of Spain.[33][34] After Giorgione [edit]The long dominance of Titian in the Venetian painting scene could be a problem for other ambitious Venetian painters. Palma Vecchio (c. 1480–1528) was slightly older than Titian, and apparently content to follow in the wake of the two great innovators; many easel paintings long attributed to Titian may actually be by him.[35] His great-nephew, Palma il Giovane (1548/50–1628), Titian's pupil, much later played a similar role, using the styles of Tintoretto and Veronese.[36] Lorenzo Lotto (c. 1480–1556/57) was born in the city, but spent most of his mature career in the terraferma, especially Bergamo. He painted religious subjects and portraits in a highly individual and sometimes eccentric style, which despite their rich colouring have a restlessness that is at odds with the Venetian mainstream.[37] Sebastiano del Piombo (c. 1485–1547) accepted a good commission in Rome in 1511, and never worked in Venice again. But in Rome he soon found that Michelangelo was equally dominant, and began a long and complicated relationship with him; eventually they fell out. His style combined Venetian colour and Roman classical grandeur, and did something to spread Venetian style to the new centre of Italian painting.[38] Paolo Veronese (1528–1588), from Verona in the Venetian terraferma, came to Venice in 1553, once he was established, commissioned to paint huge fresco schemes for the Doge's Palace, and stayed for the rest of his career. Although Tintoretto is sometimes classified as a Mannerist artist,[39] he also incorporates Venetian and individualistic aspects. In his Miracle of the Slave (1548), the Mannerist features include the crowded scene, the twisting linking of figures (as in the central figures, from the foreshortened slave on the ground to the miraculous figure of St. Mark in the sky, through the turbaned, grey-robed figure), and the drama in the gestures and poses. But the colouring maintains the warm reds, golds and greens of the Venetian school, and the figures are arranged in real three-dimensional space, in contrast to the more compressed compositions of many Mannerist works, and with its intensely theatrical, stage-like display his painting is a forerunner of the Baroque.[40] Jacopo Bassano (c. 1510–1592), followed by the four sons in his workshop, developed a rustic style which he practiced for decades from his small hometown of Bassano del Grappa, some 65 km from Venice.[41] His sons continued to work in it long after his death; Baroque painting was very slow to appeal to the Venetian market.[42] These are a few of the most outstanding in the great number of artists in the Venetian tradition, many originally from outside the Republic's territory. - The Bravo, an example of a painting often attributed to Titian or Giorgione, but also to Palma Vecchio[43] - La Bella, Palma Vecchio, 1518-20 - Sebastiano del Piombo, Visitation, 1518–19 - Andrea Schiavone, Judgement of Midas, c. 1548–50 - Jacopo Bassano, The Way to Calvary, c. 1540 17th century [edit]The 17th century was a low point in Venetian painting, especially in the first decades when Palma Giovane, Domenico Tintoretto (the son), the Bassani sons, Padovanino and others continued to turn out works essentially in the styles of the previous century. The most significant artists working in the city were all immigrants: Domenico Fetti (c. 1589–1623) from Rome, Bernardo Strozzi (c. 1581–1644) from Genoa, and the north German Johann Liss (c. 1590? – c. 1630). All were aware of the Baroque painting of Rome or Genoa, and in different ways developed styles reflecting and uniting these and traditional Venetian handling of paint and colour.[44] New directions were taken by two individual painters, Francesco Maffei from Vicenza (c. 1600–60) and Sebastiano Mazzoni from Florence (1611–78), who both worked mainly in Venice or the terraferma in unorthodox and free Baroque styles, both marked by the Venetian trait of bravura brushwork.[45] Visits to Venice by the leading Neapolitan painter Luca Giordano in 1653 and 1685 left a body of work in the latest Baroque style, and had an energising effect on younger artists such as Giovan Battista Langetti, Pietro Liberi, Antonio Molinari, and the German Johann Carl Loth.[46] - Francesco Maffei, Rinaldo's Conquest of the Enchanted Forest, 1650–55 - Sebastiano Mazzoni, Annunciation, c. 1650 18th century [edit]At the end of the 17th century things began to change dramatically, and for much of the 18th century Venetian painters were in remarkable demand all over Europe, even as the city itself declined and was a much reduced market, in particular for large works;[47] "Venetian art had become, by the mid-eighteenth century, a commodity primarily for export."[48] The first significant artist in the new style was Sebastiano Ricci (1659–1734), from Belluno in the terraferma, who trained in Venice before leaving under a cloud. He returned for a decade in 1698, and then again at the end of his life, after time in England, France and elsewhere. Drawing especially on Veronese, he developed a light, airy, Baroque style that foreshadowed the painting of most of the rest of the century, and was a great influence on young Venetian painters.[49] Giovanni Antonio Pellegrini was influenced by Ricci, and worked with his nephew Marco Ricci, but also by the later Roman Baroque. His career was mostly spent away from the city, working in several countries north of the Alps, where the new Venetian style was greatly in demand for decorating houses. It was actually slower to be accepted in Venice itself. Jacopo Amigoni (a. 1685–1752) was another travelling Venetian decorator of palaces, who was also popular for proto-Rococo portraits. He ended as a court painter in Madrid.[50] Rosalba Carriera (1675–1757), the most significant Venetian woman artist, was purely a portraitist, mostly in pastel, where she was an important technical innovator, preparing the way for this important 18th-century form. She achieved great international success, in particular in London, Paris and Vienna.[51] Giovanni Battista Tiepolo (1696–1770) is the last great Venetian painter, who was also in demand all over Europe, and painted two of his largest fresco schemes in the Würzburg Residence in northern Bavaria (1750–53) and the Royal Palace of Madrid, where he died in 1770.[52] The final flowering also included the varied talents of Giambattista Pittoni, Canaletto, Giovan Battista Piazzetta, and Francesco Guardi, as well as Giovanni Domenico Tiepolo, the most distinguished of several of the family to train with and assist Giovanni Battista Tiepolo.[53] Canaletto, his pupil and nephew Bernardo Bellotto, Michele Marieschi, and Guardi specialized in landscape painting, painting two distinct types: firstly vedute or detailed and mostly accurate panoramic views, usually of the city itself, many bought by wealthy northerners making the Grand Tour. Few Canalettos remain in Venice. The other type was the capriccio, a fanciful imaginary scene, often of classical ruins, with staffage figures. Marco Ricci was the first Venetian painter of capricci, and the form received a final development by Guardi, who produced many freely painted scenes set in the lagoon, with water, boats and land in "paintings of great tonal delicacy, whose poetic mood is tinged with nostalgia".[54] Pietro Longhi (c. 1702–1785) was Venetian painting's most significant genre painter, turning early in his career to specialize in small scenes of contemporary Venetian life, mostly with an element of gentle satire. He was one of the first Italian painters to mine this vein, and was also an early painter of conversation piece portraits. Unlike most Venetian artists, large numbers of lively sketches by him survive.[55] The death of Guardi in 1793, soon followed by the extinction of the Republic by French Revolutionary armies in 1797, effectively brought the distinctive Venetian style to an end; it had at least outlasted its rival Florence in that respect.[56] - Giovanni Antonio Pellegrini, Alexander with the Corpse of Darius, 1708 - Giovanni Battista Pittoni, The Sacrifice of Polyxena, 1733–34 - Rosalba Carriera, pastel portrait of Antoine Watteau, 1721 - Clara the rhinoceros by Pietro Longhi, 1751 Legacy [edit]The Venetian school had a great influence on subsequent painting, and the history of later Western art has been described as a dialogue between the more intellectual and sculptural/linear approach of the Florentine and Roman traditions, and the more sensual, poetic, and pleasure-seeking of the colourful Venetian school.[57] Specifically through the presence of Titians in Spain (he was careful to avoid going there in person), the Venetian style influenced later Spanish art, especially in portraits, including that of Velázquez, and through Rubens was more broadly transmitted through the rest of Europe.[58] Venice as a subject for visiting artists has been extremely popular, especially from shortly after Venetian artists ceased to be significant. Among the best known to frequently depict the city are J. M. W. Turner, James Abbott McNeill Whistler and Claude Monet.
